claims.text: As-fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure.
Phase fractions, grain-size distributions, subgrain-size distributions, and interface densities are known for the initial HfNbTiVAl10 material.
The proposed surrogate combines limited high-fidelity finite-element data, analytical micromechanics bounds, and imaging-derived microstructural descriptors.
Phase volume fractions at each scale, interface density, and grain/subgrain size distributions link the hierarchical microstructure to mechanical response.
Physics-informed constraints and data-driven interpolation across scales allow the surrogate to capture microstructure-property relationships.
The surrogate captures the relevant relationships more efficiently than full finite-element microstructural meshes.
Under room-temperature quasi-static uniaxial tensile loading, the surrogate will predict Young's modulus and 0.2% yield strength within ±5% of experiment.
Under standardized single-edge-notched-bend mode-I fracture loading, the surrogate will predict fracture toughness within ±5% of experiment.
The surrogate's computational turnaround time will be no more than 10% of that of standard full-field finite-element workflows.
Conventional high-resolution finite-element simulations on real microstructures have property-prediction errors greater than 10%.
Conventional high-resolution finite-element simulations require at least 10 hours per case.
Prediction errors will exceed 10% for microstructures containing phase compositions or damage modes outside the surrogate's training domain.
Novel precipitate phases or extensive pre-existing damage are examples of out-of-domain conditions expected to degrade model performance.
A limited high-fidelity training set creates a risk of overfitting to the initial microstructural ensemble.

contradictions.description: The central prediction requires errors within ±5% and at least a 10× speedup, but the falsification rule permits up to two specimens to exceed 10% error and does not falsify speedups between 5× and 10×. Thus, results can violate the stated hypothesis without meeting the declared falsification criterion.
